steps.title: In the ground

form.name: Ore
form.label: a few grams in every tonne

steps.text: The six platinum-group metals occur together. Most lie in a few thin layers of the Bushveld Complex in South Africa, an ancient body of once-molten rock, with more in Zimbabwe's Great Dyke. In Russia and Canada they come as a by-product of nickel and copper sulphide ore. Platinum is one of the two plentiful members of the group.

steps.title: Mine
steps.text: The South African reefs are about a metre thick and are followed more than a kilometre underground. Miners drill and blast the narrow seam and haul the rock to the shaft. It is deep, hot and labour-intensive work.

steps.title: Concentrate
steps.text: The ore is milled to powder and floated. The platinum-group metals follow the nickel and copper sulphide grains into a concentrate that is a small fraction of the rock mined.

steps.title: Smelt
steps.text: An electric furnace melts the concentrate. Silicates leave as slag and the metals collect in a matte of nickel, copper and iron sulphide. A converter burns off the iron. The nickel and copper are then leached away for sale, leaving a residue rich in precious metals.

steps.title: Refine
steps.text: The residue is dissolved in hydrochloric acid and chlorine. One by one the metals are pulled out by solvent extraction, precipitation and distillation, in a refinery where material can spend weeks or months. Platinum and palladium come out first and in the largest amounts.

steps.title: Make
steps.text: The sponge is dissolved into salts and coated onto ceramic honeycombs for catalytic converters, melted with other metals into jewellery alloy, formed into gauze for making nitric acid, or printed onto membranes for fuel cells and electrolysers.
steps.india: Johnson Matthey (Manesar) and BASF (Chennai) coat autocatalysts in India with imported metal.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: Catalytic converters take the most, chiefly on diesel vehicles, then jewellery. Platinum catalysts make fertiliser, silicones and petrol; platinum vessels melt the glass for screens and fibre. It is the catalyst in hydrogen fuel cells.
steps.india: All primary metal is imported, for vehicle catalysts, jewellery and industry.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Platinum is too valuable to throw away. Scrapped catalytic converters and old jewellery are collected and refined, and industrial users return their spent catalysts to the refiner.
steps.india: Hindustan Platinum and other refiners recover platinum-group metals from spent catalysts. A Rs 1,500 crore recycling scheme (2025) covers catalytic converters.
